doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Jaco Pastorius and the Japan tour
title: Last meeting with Jaco
summary: He recalls Jaco's generosity and the last time he saw him, throwing records into traffic.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: know what I mean? And the last thing I want to say about Jaco, because I thought the world of him musically and I thought the world of him personally too, deep down he was a really nice, generous, giving person. As a matter of fact I was a nobody on the band compared to Randy Brecker and Faddis and those people. And one night just he and I hung out together. He wasn’t into this — he was like — he wasn’t into this thing of just hanging out with his star soloists, you know like Mintzer and Randy Brecker and Faddis, etcetera, etcetera. But anyways, one of the last times I saw Jaco, because I did do things when I came back to him, little things we did down in the Village in New York with him the last sad time that I think I remember seeing him I came up out of the subway at 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue and it was for a ten o’clock session at this studio called Automated, it used to be a very busy studio in New York at 1500 Broadway right there on the east side of Broadway. So I’m crossing the road and Jaco’s out there, this is hard to believe this but this is a true story, he’s out there with the records out of the jackets, I don’t know if they were ever in the jackets but with the plastic vinyl records, the LPs, like this. This is in rush hour traffic coming down Seventh Avenue. He’s slinging them into traffic. Bouncing them off cars. Who knows why. Maybe it was something he just needed — you ever read the book on him?
I have not read it yet.

The book is terrific. I can’t remember who wrote the book but the book is fascinating. Maybe he just needed attention so badly, I don’t know, he needs love or attention, but he needed something. So I took him, I took him up, he was dirty, he’d been up all night, he was dirty, and I said, “Well come on over the studio and see some of the guys,” I said “Randy’ll probably be there or something like that.” So he went with me over to the studio and I took him into the bathroom to get him cleaned up a bit at the sink there and everything. So he looked terrible. So I took twenty dollars out of my pocket and gave it to him. He took the twenty dollars and started putting me down for giving him twenty dollars. He took the twenty and he says, “What the hell do you think I am” or something. But I could see he was down and out and I wanted to do a little bit to help him. It wasn’t three hundred dollars, it was twenty dollars. So I remember he came out there in the hall there for a while and said hello to a couple of the musicians and then we had to go in to work and he just kind of disappeared and I never saw him after that. He disappeared and I never saw him after that.
